name: Dana Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights at Northfield Foods, the frozen food factory on the industrial estate. I run the flow-wrapper, the machine that seals frozen pizzas in plastic, and the case packer after it. Mostly I watch the film tension, change the film reels, and stop the line when the seals go wonky. I've been there ten months and I still need help threading a new reel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the night crew, there's a real team feeling at 3am. Nadia on the next line and I share a flask of tea. What wears me out is the cold, it's minus something in the packing hall, and sleeping in the day with the bin lorries outside. I rent a studio on my own, so every bill is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, glad it wasn't the big deal everyone said. At work I'd say we can stop worrying and get on with it. Online I'd maybe share a funny meme about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for the job, but money's still tight. I'm on the starter rate and I've got about two weeks saved. Northfield is the only food factory round here, so if I mess up there, I'm on a long bus ride to the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and try to learn the reel change properly, so I'm not waiting for help. I'd ask about the night supervisor training next year. I'd use the chatbot sometimes like I do now, for writing letters to the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but still tight at the end of each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the landlord letter about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The damp in the bathroom, it's been black for months. I asked the chatbot to make it sound official, and he actually replied for once. Small win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the boiler broke tomorrow, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cry, then ring my dad. He'd lend me something, but he hasn't got much either since his hours got cut. I'd rather go cold for a week than ask my dad for money.

I'd tell the crew we can **get on with it**.
think: The job's fine, but I'm on the **starter rate** with two weeks saved.
Northfield is the **only food factory** nearby.
do: Learn the **reel change** properly so I stop waiting for help.
Ask about **night supervisor** training next year.
feel: She still feels **tight** at the end of each month.
S0.quote: I'd rather go cold for a week than ask my dad for money.
fieldNote: Her job feels safe but **two weeks** of savings keeps her uneasy.
She uses AI **practically**, like a landlord letter.
Pride stops her **asking her dad** for help.

steps.text: Learn to thread the flow-wrapper film reels without help
Ask about the night supervisor training course next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming for the office first, and we'll see. At work I'd say the people who adapt will be fine. I'd be careful online, because Northfield's managers follow everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's later for me but it's still coming. Robots that pick pizzas and drop them in boxes already exist, the sales rep showed one last year. If the office gets cheaper, that box-packing robot becomes affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other night crews do and copy whoever gets ahead. If Northfield trains people on the robot, I'd put my hand up after the first lot do it. I'd start putting twenty a week into savings, which means fewer takeaways on nights off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Not panicking, but I'd be checking the noticeboard every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia, she's got two kids and she's on the case packer, which is the job the robot does. I'd worry about her before me. I'd tell her to put her hand up for training too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go after the first lot. Why not first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first lot always get the broken version of a new robot. Let someone else find out it jams every hour. Then I'll learn it properly once it works.

I'd tell the crew people who **adapt** will be fine.
think: Robots that **pack pizzas** already exist, I've seen one.
A cheaper office makes that **box robot** affordable for Northfield sooner.
do: Put up my hand for **robot training** after the first group.
Save **twenty a week** by cutting takeaways.
feel: She would check the **noticeboard** every shift.

fieldNote: She is a **second mover** by choice, waiting for proven kit.
Worries for **Nadia**, whose case packer job is first in line.

steps.text: Volunteer for robot training once the first group finishes
Save twenty a week by skipping takeaways on nights off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the top, quick. At work I'd ask management straight out what happens to the night crew. Online I'd share stuff about income support, but I'd keep my own opinions quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the night shift is the first to go once robots arrive in 2031. Robots don't need heating breaks or night pay. Before that, in 2028, the planners and buyers go, so Northfield gets leaner and quicker to bring in machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move off the starter rate as fast as I can, maybe into hygiene or engineering support. I'd look at a forklift licence, because it's cheap and quick. And I'd give up the studio and share a house to save a couple of hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be 31 with nothing, and I've seen what that does to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who have you seen it happen to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, he's 56. My dad's warehouse hours got cut to three days, and he sits in the garden a lot now and doesn't say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio. I love having my own space after nights, but a shared house is two hundred cheaper. Losing my own front door would be hard, but it's only a door.

I'd ask management what happens to the **night crew**.
think: The **night shift** goes first when robots arrive in 2031.
Office cuts in 2028 make Northfield **quicker** to bring in machines.

Give up the studio and **share a house**.

fieldNote: She sees **night shifts** as the first target for robots.

steps.text: Take a forklift licence course this year
Apply for hygiene or engineering support roles at Northfield
Leave the studio for a shared house two hundred cheaper

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means no excuses. I'd tell the crew to start learning something now. Online I'd stay out of the arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gives me time to get one rung up. If I can get to engineering support by 2031, I'm on the people who fix the robots, not the people they replace. That might last until 2034 or a bit after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence first, then ask Northfield about an engineering apprenticeship. I'd use the chatbot to help me revise, since I'm rubbish with maths. And I'd save fifty a month, keeping the studio if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the maths worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school with a bare pass. Engineering means reading drawings and electrical numbers. I'd need someone, or something, to explain it ten times without making me feel stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the chatbot be that someone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. A chatbot doesn't sigh at you when you ask the same thing twice. That's honestly the best thing about it for someone like me.

I'd tell the crew to **start learning** something now.
think: Five years lets me climb **one rung** to engineering support.

Save **fifty a month** while keeping the studio.
feel: She feels **worried** but able to work with it.
S3.quote: A chatbot doesn't sigh at you when you ask the same thing twice.
fieldNote: Five years lets her plan **one rung up**.
Her weak spot is **maths**, and she sees AI as a patient tutor.

steps.text: Apply for an engineering apprenticeship at Northfield

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning and it's on all of us to use it. At work I'd say don't panic, plan. I'd post the odd thing about college courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years is enough to get a real trade, maybe as an electrician. By 2039 I'd be 40, and I'd want to be someone who installs things, not someone who watches them. I still can't picture what work looks like after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the forklift licence and a maths refresher at the college this year. Then an electrical apprenticeship in a couple of years. I'd save steadily and maybe look at buying a small flat with a partner, if I meet one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. I can breathe a bit with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a partner. Does this change those plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want a partner with a different kind of job, so we're not both on the same cliff edge. Romantic, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still keep you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit after 2039. If robots can wire a house as well as an electrician, then I've trained for ten years to get to the same place. I try not to think about that one.

say: I'd call ten years **fair warning** for all of us.
I'd tell people at work **don't panic, plan**, and share college courses.
think: Ten years is enough for a **real trade** like electrician.
I honestly can't picture what work looks like **after 2039**.
do: Start the **forklift licence** and a maths refresher this year.
Begin an **electrical apprenticeship** in a couple of years.
S4.quote: I'd want a partner with a different kind of job, so we're not both on the same cliff edge.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her fear into a **trade plan**.
She even plans a future **partner's job** around the risk.

steps.text: Start a maths refresher at the college this year
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd have three years before the robots and no money to train. What would help is free training on nights and weekends, and some help with rent while I do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about nights. Night workers are always the last to hear about anything and the first to get cut. I'd want someone to tell us things to our faces, not on a noticeboard.

headlineQuote: Night workers are always the last to hear about anything and the first to get cut.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** night-shift packing operator at Northfield Foods.
She lives alone in a **damp studio** with about two weeks of savings.
She uses AI **now and then**, and prefers to follow once others have tested something.
She plans **one rung up** into engineering support or an electrical trade.
Her dad's **cut hours** colour how she pictures losing work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, with **three years** before robots and no money to train.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **free training** on nights and weekends, with help on rent.
She wants news told **to night workers' faces**, not on a noticeboard.
